source.title: Synthetic vs Real: Deep Learning on Controlled Noise
source.authors: Lu Jiang; Di Huang; Weilong Yang

record.file_problem: The supplied text contains the paper and supplementary materials. It has some flattened tables, but the results relevant to the claim are described in text or shown in identified figures.
record.tranche_reason: The study trains vanilla networks on controlled synthetic and web label noise, then compares generalization and peak-to-final accuracy. It tests related noisy-label behavior with different settings, but does not reproduce training on completely random labels.
record.gate_note: The study reports training and validation accuracy curves at 50% noise in Figure 1 and validation curves in Figure 2, but does not report results for completely random labels. Results cited from Zhang et al. and Arpit et al. are not this study’s own results. No results test shuffled pixels or Gaussian-noise inputs, optimization time versus true labels, explicit regularization on random labels, or label memorization order directly.
record.test_reason: Vanilla-network experiments on two additional datasets bear on V4's test-performance component under symmetric random label corruption. Complete random labeling and perfect training fit across noise levels are not established. Peak-to-final validation gaps do not establish V6's ordering of clean-pattern learning and noisy-label memorization.
record.authors_conclusion: The record accurately summarizes the authors' relevant conclusions: DNNs generalize better on controlled web noise than on synthetic noise, and the authors suggest they may not learn patterns first on web noise, especially in fine-grained classification. The latter is their interpretation of validation gaps, rather than a direct measurement of memorization order.
record.recipe_differences: Controlled label-noise experiments on Mini-ImageNet and Stanford Cars using vanilla training; noise is capped at 80%, and the study compares synthetic and web noise rather than fully random labels.
record.method_sensitivity: Noise type (synthetic versus web), dataset (Mini-ImageNet versus Stanford Cars), and training setting (from scratch versus fine-tuning) change the reported generalization or peak-to-final accuracy patterns.

fits_no_version.finding: Validation performance deteriorates less under web noise than under synthetic symmetric noise.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Networks are more robust to these controlled, instance-dependent web-label errors than to uniform random label corruption.

fits_no_version.finding: Peak-to-final clean-validation drops are generally smaller for web noise, particularly on Stanford Cars.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Early stopping offers less validation-performance benefit under the tested web noise; this statistic alone does not determine memorization order.

record.problems: The claim-relevant accuracy curves are figures without exact values in the supplied text. Peak-to-final validation accuracy is an indirect indicator of pattern learning, and the study tests noise only up to 80%, not completely random labels.
record.rows_left_out: No additional rows. The accuracy curves and performance-drop results are included as figure-only rows because the supplied text does not give exact plotted values.

untested.parts: Completely random labeling, near-zero training error under that condition, chance test performance, and unchanged architecture and hyperparameters.
Relative time to fit true versus random labels and convergence slowdown as corruption increases.
Fitting shuffled pixels, independently permuted pixels, and Gaussian-noise inputs.
Perfect training fit at every corruption level; the fully random endpoint; and direct evidence that remaining signal is captured while noise is memorized.
Whether explicit regularizers prevent fitting fully random labels and whether removing them alone preserves true-label generalization.
The temporal ordering of fitting shared real-data patterns versus noisy labels. Validation gaps are an indirect interpretation, without separate fitting trajectories for clean and corrupted examples.

missing.what: Record the complete vanilla final-validation accuracy series at all ten synthetic-noise levels. These numerical results establish the across-noise degradation more directly than the existing 0%-versus-40% figure rows. The record incorrectly says exact values are unavailable.
missing.locator: Appendix D, Tables 4–7, Vanilla columns; Stanford Cars table captions contain a duplicated training-setting description

record.verdict_notes: The study is not an original source of these versions. Synthetic corruption selects an incorrect class uniformly, excluding the true class. Web-noise conditions also change the images and can include classes outside the target vocabulary. Neither weaker web-noise degradation nor unmeasured endpoints warrant limits_scope verdicts on V4.

versions.untested_parts: Completely random labeling; zero or near-zero training error at that condition; test error at chance.
Training time relative to true labels and convergence as corrupted-label fraction grows.
Shuffled pixels, independently permuted pixels, and Gaussian-noise inputs.
The study varies noise from 0% to 80%, not all labels corrupted; it does not establish perfect training fit at each level or test error at chance.
Whether weight decay, dropout, or augmentation prevent fitting completely random labels, and whether removing them alone harms true-label generalization.
The study measures peak-to-final validation accuracy drops, not the time course of fitting real versus completely random labels directly.

rows.note: The text describes a palpable validation-performance degradation for blue noise after training converges; plotted values are not transcribed in the supplied text.
rows.check: Observed for the test-degradation component only. Appendix D Table 5 supplies exact vanilla final validation accuracies: 72.8% at 0% noise, 43.5% at 40%, and 14.0% at 80%. Missing training-fit evidence does not itself make this measured degradation partial.

rows.subject: Inception-ResNet-v2
rows.operation_detail: Compared peak and final clean-validation accuracy across noise levels.
rows.measure: Relative drop from peak to final validation accuracy
rows.value: Figure only; described as a significant drop as noise level grows
rows.uncertainty: 95% confidence interval shown in Figure 2; exact values not stated
rows.note: The text says the blue curves show a significant drop as noise grows, consistent with Arpit et al.’s finding on synthetic noise.
rows.check: A peak-to-final clean-validation drop measures generalization over training, not when clean and noisy training examples are fitted. It cannot establish V6. Appendix D Table 5 also provides exact peak/final values, so the result is not exclusively figure-only.

rows.subject: Inception-ResNet-v2
rows.operation_detail: Compared peak and final clean-validation accuracy across noise levels.
rows.measure: Relative drop from peak to final validation accuracy
rows.value: Figure only; described as considerably smaller than blue-noise drop
rows.uncertainty: 95% confidence interval shown in Figure 2; exact values not stated
rows.note: The peak-to-final validation gap is used as an indirect indicator of early pattern learning, not a direct measure of when examples are memorized.
rows.check: A smaller validation drop does not show a weaker clean-first memorization order. Exact vanilla peak/final values appear in Appendix D Table 5. Figure 2's confidence belt across noise levels is not uncertainty for this peak-to-final statistic.

rows.subject: Inception-ResNet-v2
rows.operation_detail: Compared peak and final clean-validation accuracy across noise levels.
rows.measure: Relative drop from peak to final validation accuracy
rows.value: Figure only; described as a significant drop as noise level grows
rows.uncertainty: 95% confidence interval shown in Figure 2; exact values not stated
rows.note: The text says the blue curves show a significant drop as noise grows, consistent with Arpit et al.’s finding on synthetic noise.
rows.check: Validation deterioration cannot determine the temporal ordering in V6. The general description of a significant blue-noise drop should not be assigned uniformly to this condition: Appendix D Table 7's scratch series has peak/final accuracy 40.4/37.2 at 40% noise and 3.1/1.3 at 80%.

rows.subject: Inception-ResNet-v2
rows.operation_detail: Compared peak and final clean-validation accuracy across noise levels.
rows.measure: Relative drop from peak to final validation accuracy
rows.value: Figure only; described as considerably smaller and approaching zero
rows.uncertainty: 95% confidence interval shown in Figure 2; exact values not stated
rows.note: The authors say this suggests DNNs may not learn patterns first on red noise, at least for fine-grained classification.
rows.check: Near-zero validation decline does not establish absence of pattern-first learning. Appendix D Table 7 reports exact scratch peak/final values, including 77.4/76.9 at 40% web noise and 43.3/43.0 at 80%. The cited confidence belt does not quantify uncertainty in this statistic.

relationships.condition: Symmetric synthetic label noise from 0% to 80%; Inception-ResNet-v2 on Mini-ImageNet and Stanford Cars, from scratch and fine-tuned
relationships.reason: R1, R3, R5, and R7 support the tested degradation component: the vanilla final-validation series decline steadily as random corruption increases. They do not establish perfect training fit or the fully random endpoint.
relationships.display_finding: Final validation accuracy declined steadily as random corruption increased on Mini-ImageNet and Stanford Cars under both initialization settings.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.
